questions.stem: At room temperature and pressure (RTP), one mole of any gas occupies:
questions.explanation: At room temperature and pressure (approximately 20°C and 1 atmosphere), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³). This is called the molar gas volume. The value 22.4 dm³ is at standard temperature and pressure (0°C and 1 atm), which is different from RTP. At GCSE, use 24 dm³ at RTP.

questions.stem: What volume does 0.5 moles of oxygen gas occupy at RTP?
questions.explanation: Volume = moles x molar volume = 0.5 x 24 = 12 dm³. Since 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP, half a mole occupies half of 24 dm³ = 12 dm³. This applies to any gas - the type of gas does not matter because at RTP, all gases behave similarly.

questions.stem: 4.4 g of carbon dioxide gas (Mr = 44) is at RTP. What volume does it occupy?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate moles = mass / Mr = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol. Step 2: Volume = moles x 24 = 0.1 x 24 = 2.4 dm³. First convert mass to moles, then use the molar volume to find the volume. This two-step approach is essential for gas volume calculations.

questions.stem: A gas syringe collects 120 cm³ of hydrogen gas at RTP. How many moles of hydrogen is this?
questions.explanation: Convert cm³ to dm³: 120 cm³ = 0.12 dm³. Moles = volume / molar volume = 0.12 / 24 = 0.005 mol. Alternatively, since 24 dm³ = 24,000 cm³: moles = 120 / 24,000 = 0.005 mol. Always ensure your volume units match the molar volume units.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, what volume of hydrogen gas is produced at RTP when 6.5 g of zinc reacts? [Ar: Zn = 65]
questions.explanation: Step 1: Moles of Zn = 6.5/65 = 0.1 mol. Step 2: From the equation, 1 mol Zn produces 1 mol H₂ (1:1 ratio), so 0.1 mol Zn produces 0.1 mol H₂. Step 3: Volume of H₂ = 0.1 x 24 = 2.4 dm³. This combines moles from mass, equation ratios, and molar gas volume.
